description: Arjuna, given a divine eye, sees the whole universe gathered in one body with countless faces and eyes, brighter than a thousand suns, and the warriors rushing into its mouths; his hair stands on end, he is filled with wonder and then with fear.
At the sight of his kinsmen Arjuna's limbs fail, his mouth dries, his body trembles, his hair stands on end, the bow slips from his hand, his skin burns and his mind reels.
The mind of the yogin who practises the yoga of the self is steady like a lamp that does not flicker in a windless place.

When the mind comes to rest one sees the self by the self and is content; one knows an endless happiness grasped by the intellect beyond the senses, is not shaken even by great sorrow, and attains the happiness of contact with Brahman.
Signs of the prevailing guṇa: light of knowledge through all the gates of the body (sattva); greed, activity, restlessness and longing (rajas); darkness, inertia, negligence and delusion (tamas).

The one beyond the guṇas neither hates their effects when present nor longs for them when absent, sits as one indifferent, and is the same in pleasure and pain, praise and blame, honour and dishonour.
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled sage is awake in; what beings are awake in is night for the seeing sage.
In the Kaurava court Kṛṣṇa laughs and from his lightning-like body emerge thumb-sized gods blazing like fire — Brahmā, Rudra, the Ādityas, Vasus, Maruts, Indra, yakṣas, gandharvas and rākṣasas.
In the dissolution Mārkaṇḍeya sees a divine child on a banyan branch in the one ocean, is drawn into its mouth, and sees within its body the whole world.
Nārada in the White Island sees the white one-pointed devotees and receives a vision of Nārāyaṇa in universal form, a sight the Lord says even Brahmā has not had.
Through Vyāsa's gift Sañjaya sees and knows everything in the battle, in open or in secret, even thoughts.
Bhīṣma holds his life-breaths until the sun's northern course; at death his self, restrained in all the openings, breaks through the crown of the head and rises to heaven.
At his death Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira's body by yoga — limbs into limbs, breaths into breaths, senses into senses.
The yoginī Sulabhā, versed in yoga, enters king Janaka's understanding 'sattva by sattva'.
Yogins endowed with yoga-power check the sense-objects as an elephant stems a current and, as lords, enter Prajāpatis, seers, gods and the great elements at will.
Śuka rises by yoga from the peak of Kailāsa into the sky and passes beyond, while the mountains and trees answer Vyāsa's cry.
Jaigīṣavya is seen by Asita Devala to arrive by yoga at distant places before him and to move among the worlds.
